params.title: RADAR Principles
params.subtitle: How pulse RADAR measures range, the timing, power and wavelength math, and the circuits in Figures 8A1 to 8A8.

onScreen: Pulse timing, power and wavelength math
scenes.narration: Welcome to RADAR principles. RADAR stands for radio detection and ranging. In this lesson you'll see how a pulse RADAR measures range, and how pulse timing, power and frequency fit together. We'll walk through the radar mile, average power, duty cycle, pulse repetition frequency and wavelength calculations one line at a time. Then we'll identify the receiver, logic and digital circuits shown in the pool figures, 8A1 through 8A8. Let's start with the main parts of a marine RADAR system.

params.title: The RADAR system's timing and signal path

blocks.label: Synchronizer
blocks.note: Timer or trigger generator: sets timing

blocks.label: Indicator
blocks.note: One sweep per pulse: PRF sets sweep rate

onScreen: Duplexer: one antenna for transmit and receive
Indicator: one sweep per pulse, so PRF sets the sweep rate
scenes.narration: The synchronizer, also called the timer or trigger generator, controls timing throughout the RADAR system. It produces the pulses that fire the modulator, which pulses the magnetron. The magnetron's pulse goes to the duplexer. The duplexer allows a single antenna to be used for both transmitting and receiving. During each pulse, it routes the energy to the antenna and blocks the receiver. At the same instant the modulator fires, the synchronizer starts the indicator sweep and range circuits. Each transmitted pulse triggers one sweep, so the sweep frequency of the indicator is set by the pulse repetition frequency, or PRF. Carrier frequency and pulse width don't decide how often the trace restarts. Between pulses, the duplexer passes the weak returning echoes to the receiver, and on to the indicator.

params.title: Echo size and maximum range
items: Echo size: transmitted power, antenna effective area, transmit and receive losses
Also the target's RADAR cross section and the range to target
Receiver gain is not one: it only amplifies an echo after it arrives
Carrier frequency, PRF and receiver sensitivity affect maximum range
Recovery time has no effect on maximum range: it limits minimum range

onScreen: Echo size: power, antenna area, losses, RADAR cross section, range
Maximum range: carrier frequency, PRF, receiver sensitivity
Recovery time: no effect on maximum range; limits minimum range
scenes.narration: What decides how big a target's echo is? The radar range equation answers that. The size of the echo is controlled by the transmitted power, the antenna's effective area, the transmit and receive losses, the RADAR cross section of the target, and the range to the target. Receiver gain is not on that list: it only amplifies an echo after it arrives. Now maximum range. Carrier frequency, PRF and receiver sensitivity all affect it. Recovery time has no effect on maximum range. Recovery time is how quickly the TR tube, the transmit-receive tube, and the receiver regain full sensitivity after each pulse. So it limits the minimum range, not the maximum.

params.title: Peak power versus average power
labels: Peak power: the power during the brief pulse itself
Pulse width: how long each pulse lasts
Average power: the peak spread over the whole repetition period
P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>peak</sub> × pulse width × PRF

onScreen: Average power: spread over the repetition period
P avg = P peak × pulse width × PRF
scenes.narration: Here's a RADAR pulse train. Peak power is the power during the brief pulse itself. The pulse width is how long each pulse lasts, and then the transmitter rests until the next one. Average power is the transmitter power measured over a period of time: the peak pulse power spread over the whole repetition period. So P sub average equals P sub peak, times the pulse width, times the PRF. Because each pulse is so short, the average power is far lower than the peak. We'll come back to this pulse train whenever pulse width, PRF or duty cycle comes up.

params.title: The RADAR mile
labels: A target 1 nautical mile away
Out and back: 12.34 µs, 1 RADAR mile
One way: about 6.17 µs per nautical mile
3 nautical miles one way: 3 × 6.17 µs = 18.51 µs

onScreen: Out and back: 12.34 µs, 1 RADAR mile
One way: about 6.17 µs per nautical mile
scenes.narration: Range is all about timing. A RADAR pulse travels out to a target 1 nautical mile away and back again in 12.34 microseconds. That round trip time is called 1 RADAR mile: 12.34 microseconds. One way, a radio wave covers 1 nautical mile in about 6.17 microseconds, half the RADAR mile. So a signal traveling one way to a point 3 nautical miles away takes 3 times 6.17 microseconds, or 18.51 microseconds.

params.title: Meters of range per microsecond
steps: Radio waves travel about 300 meters per µs
The echo goes out and back: divide by 2

onScreen: Radio waves: about 300 meters per µs
scenes.narration: Here's another constant the exam likes. Radio waves travel about 300 meters every microsecond. But the echo has to go out and come back, so each microsecond of echo delay covers only half that distance in range. 300 divided by 2 gives 150 meters of range per microsecond. Remember the units: RADAR range is measured by the constant 150 meters per microsecond, meters, not yards.

params.title: Echo time and range
steps: Reverse it: R = t ÷ 12.34 µs, no halving

scenes.narration: To find echo time, multiply the range by the RADAR mile: t equals range times 12.34 microseconds. A target 5 miles away: 5 times 12.34 is 61.7 microseconds. A target 10 nautical miles away: 10 times 12.34 is 123.4 microseconds. Going the other way, range is echo time divided by the RADAR mile. Don't halve anything, because 12.34 microseconds is already a round trip. An echo that returns after 308.5 microseconds: 308.5 divided by 12.34 gives a range of 25 nautical miles.

params.title: Marine RADAR bands in the SHF range

marks.label: S-band, near 3 GHz
marks.note: Band 2 to 4 GHz: about 15 to 7.5 cm

onScreen: S-band: 2 to 4 GHz, marine sets near 3 GHz
X-band: 8 to 12 GHz, marine sets near 9.4 GHz
scenes.narration: Marine RADAR frequencies are in the SHF, or super high frequency, part of the radio spectrum: 3 to 30 gigahertz. Marine sets use mainly two bands. An S-band RADAR operates in the 2 to 4 gigahertz band, wavelengths of about 15 down to 7.5 centimeters, and marine S-band sets typically run near 3 gigahertz. An X-band RADAR operates in the 8 to 12 gigahertz band. Marine X-band sets usually transmit near 9.4 gigahertz, a wavelength of about 3.2 centimeters.

Wavelength, lambda, equals the speed of light, c, divided by frequency, f. For a 3 gigahertz RADAR: 3 times 10 to the power 8 meters per second, divided by 3 times 10 to the power 9 hertz, gives 0.1 meter, or 10 centimeters. That's why S-band is called 10-centimeter radar. Short wavelengths like this are why practical RADAR uses microwave frequencies: they produce stronger target echoes. A wavelength of a few centimeters is small compared with ships, buoys and coastlines, so they reflect strongly. And a practical-size antenna can form a narrow, high-gain beam.

Let's compare the two bands. S-band runs from 2 to 4 gigahertz, with a wavelength of about 10 centimeters. X-band runs from 8 to 12 gigahertz, about 3 centimeters. The major advantage of S-band over X-band is that it is less affected by weather conditions. Its longer wavelength is scattered and absorbed far less by rain, snow and fog. But watch the trap: X-band, not S-band, has the better bearing resolution.

params.title: Duty cycle and the pulse period
labels: Duty cycle = PW × PRF: the fraction of time the transmitter is on
A 100 kW pulse, 0.5 µs wide, every 1600 µs
PRF only 625 Hz; duty cycle only 0.03125 percent

scenes.narration: Back to our pulse train. Average power is peak power times duty cycle. Duty cycle is the fraction of time the transmitter is on, which is the pulse width, PW, times the PRF. So P sub average equals P sub peak times PW times PRF. You can also find average power as peak power times pulse width, divided by the pulse period. Take a 0.5 microsecond, 100 kilowatt pulse sent every 1600 microseconds. 100,000 watts times 0.5 microseconds, divided by 1,600 microseconds, gives 31.25 watts. That's a PRF of only 625 hertz, and a duty cycle of only 0.03125 percent.

onScreen: P avg = P pk × PW × PRF
1000 Hz, 1 µs, 100 kW: 100 W, duty cycle 0.001
scenes.narration: Now the exam's average power problems. First: a PRF of 400 hertz, a 1 microsecond pulse, and 100 kilowatts peak. 100,000 watts times 1 times 10 to the power minus 6 seconds, times 400 hertz, equals 40 watts. Second: a PRF of 900 hertz, a 0.5 microsecond pulse, and 15 kilowatts peak. 15,000 watts times 0.5 times 10 to the power minus 6 seconds, times 900 hertz, equals 6.75 watts. Third: a PRF of 1000 hertz, a 1 microsecond pulse, and 100 kilowatts peak. 100,000 watts times 1 times 10 to the power minus 6 seconds, times 1,000 hertz, equals 100 watts. That's a duty cycle of 0.001.

Duty cycle on its own: with a PRF of 1,000 hertz and a 0.5 microsecond pulse, the duty cycle is 0.5 times 10 to the power minus 6 seconds, times 1,000 hertz, or 0.0005. The question may also give you the peak power and minimum range, but you don't need them. Now turn the formula around to find peak power. P sub peak equals P sub average, divided by PW times PRF. With 18 watts average, a 1 microsecond pulse and a PRF of 900 hertz: 18 watts divided by 1 times 10 to the power minus 6 seconds times 900 hertz. That's 18 divided by 0.0009, which is 20,000 watts, or 20 kilowatts.

params.title: Highest PRF for a given range
steps: Each echo must return before the next pulse

onScreen: Echo returns before the next pulse
scenes.narration: Range also limits how fast pulses can be sent. Each echo must return before the next pulse fires. So the pulse period must be at least the round trip time, t equals range times 12.34 microseconds, and the PRF must be no more than 1 divided by t. For a range of 5 nautical miles: t equals 5 times 12.34, or 61.7 microseconds. 1 divided by 61.7 microseconds is about 16.2 kilohertz. So the PRF should be 16.2 kilohertz or less.

The same steps work for any range. 5 nautical miles gave 16.2 kilohertz. For 10 nautical miles, t is 10 times 12.34, or 123.4 microseconds, so the PRF should be approximately 8.1 kilohertz or less. For 30 nautical miles, t is 30 times 12.34, or 370.2 microseconds, so the PRF should be 2.7 kilohertz or less. For 100 nautical miles, t is 100 times 12.34, or 1,234 microseconds, so the PRF should be 810 hertz or less. Notice the pattern: the longer the range, the lower the maximum PRF.

params.title: Minimum range and pulse width
labels: A target very close in hides inside the transmitted pulse
While the pulse is on, the receiver is protected and can't hear echoes
Minimum range: about 150 m per µs of pulse width
Short range RADARs: narrow pulses at a fast rate

onScreen: Close target hidden inside the pulse
About 150 m of minimum range per µs of pulse width
Short range: narrow pulses at a fast rate
scenes.narration: The minimum range of a RADAR is determined by the transmitted pulse width. A target very close in is hidden inside the transmitted pulse, because while the pulse is on, the receiver is protected and can't hear echoes. That works out to about 150 meters of minimum range for every microsecond of pulse width. That's why short range RADARs most likely transmit narrow pulses at a fast rate. Narrow pulses give a small minimum range and fine range resolution. And close-in echoes return quickly, so pulses can be sent often.

onScreen: 0.05 µs pulse at 2000 Hz: duty cycle 0.0001
scenes.narration: The pulse repetition interval, or PRI, is the time from the start of one pulse to the start of the next. It's the reciprocal of the PRF: PRI equals 1 divided by PRF. A PRF of 2500 hertz gives 1 divided by 2,500, which is 0.0004 seconds, or 400 microseconds. A PRF of 2000 hertz gives 1 divided by 2,000, which is 0.0005 seconds, or 500 microseconds. Now add a pulse width of 0.05 microseconds at that 2000 hertz PRF. Duty cycle equals PW times PRF: 0.05 times 10 to the power minus 6 seconds, times 2,000 hertz, equals 0.0001. The transmitter is on for only a tiny fraction of the time.

params.title: Pulse width and PRR go opposite ways
labels: Lower PRR with wider pulse width
Long range: wider pulses at a lower PRR
Lower PRR: time for distant echoes, duty cycle kept in limits
Short range: the opposite, narrow pulses at a higher PRR

onScreen: Lower PRR with wider pulse width
Long range: wide pulses, lower PRR
Time for distant echoes; average power in limits
Short range: narrow pulses, higher PRR
scenes.narration: The pulse repetition rate, or PRR, and the pulse width go opposite ways: lower PRR with wider pulse width. This pulse train shows a long-range setting. It uses wider pulses and lowers the PRR. The lower rate allows time for distant echoes to return, and it keeps the duty cycle and the magnetron's average power within limits. Short-range settings do the opposite: narrow pulses at a higher PRR.

params.title: What the PRR is, and seeing small targets
items: PRR is the pulse rate of the magnetron: how many times per second it fires
The receiver's local oscillator, klystron or solid-state, runs continuously, not pulsed
Small targets: use a long pulse width with high output power
More energy on target gives an echo strong enough to stand out above receiver noise

onScreen: Small targets: long pulse, high power
Echo stands out above receiver noise
scenes.narration: What exactly is the PRR? It's the pulse rate of the magnetron: how many times per second the magnetron is fired. It is not the receiver's local oscillator. That oscillator, whether a klystron or solid-state, runs continuously and is not pulsed. One more exam favorite: small targets are best detected using a long pulse width with high output power. A long, powerful pulse puts more energy on the target, and gives an echo strong enough to stand out above the receiver noise.

callouts.label: Block 46: the TR box, between the waveguide and the crystal detector
It fires during the transmitted pulse to protect the crystal
The rest of the time, it passes the weak echoes
Block 47: the RF attenuator, fed straight from the magnetron
Cuts a sample of the output to a safe level for the AFC mixer

onScreen: Fires during the pulse to protect the crystal
Block 47: RF attenuator from the magnetron
Safe sample for the AFC mixer
scenes.narration: Here's Figure 8A1. Block 46 is the TR box, the transmit-receive switch. It sits between the waveguide and the receiver's crystal detector. During the transmitted pulse, the TR box fires to protect the fragile crystal. The rest of the time, it passes the weak echoes through. Block 47 is the RF, or radio frequency, attenuator. It's fed straight from the magnetron, and it cuts a small sample of the powerful transmitter output down to a safe level for the AFC mixer. AFC stands for automatic frequency control.

blocks.label: Output buffer
blocks.note: Amplifier: load can't drain the capacitor

onScreen: Input buffer charges the capacitor quickly
Analog switch: connects, then opens to freeze
Output buffer protects the held voltage
scenes.narration: A basic sample-and-hold circuit contains an analog switch, a capacitor, amplifiers, and input and output buffers. The signal enters through the input buffer, an amplifier that can charge the hold capacitor quickly. The analog switch connects the signal to the hold capacitor. When the switch opens, the voltage on the capacitor is frozen: that's the hold. Finally, the output buffer keeps the load from draining the capacitor, so the held voltage stays put.

params.title: TTL and CMOS NAND gates compared
rows: Upper transistor of the totem-pole output

scenes.narration: Now compare a TTL NAND gate with a CMOS NAND gate. TTL means transistor-transistor logic, and CMOS means complementary metal-oxide semiconductor. Both have active pull-up outputs. TTL pulls its output high through the upper transistor of its totem-pole output. CMOS does it through P-channel MOSFETs, metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transistors. And neither one is a three-state device. So what they have in common is active pull-up.

params.title: Handling silicon crystals
items: Mixer and detector crystals are fragile point-contact diodes
Very sensitive to static electric charges
Store them wrapped in lead foil
Only very low currents: about 3 mA is typical
Much higher current would burn out the tiny junction

onScreen: Higher current burns out the junction
scenes.narration: Silicon mixer and detector crystals are fragile point-contact diodes, and every caution applies. They are very sensitive to static electric charges. They should be wrapped in lead foil for storage. And they tolerate only very low currents. A typical current for a silicon crystal in a RADAR mixer or detector circuit is 3 milliamps. Much higher currents would burn out the tiny junction.

params.title: The Gunn oscillator
items: The resonant cavity is the basic frequency-determining element
The Gunn diode supplies the negative resistance that sustains oscillation
Supply voltage and loading only pull the frequency slightly
Uses both negative resistance and the bulk effect: no PN junction
At high fields, electrons in the gallium arsenide move to a slower energy band

onScreen: Supply voltage and loading: slight pull only
scenes.narration: Now two microwave oscillators. In a Gunn oscillator, the basic frequency-determining element is the resonant cavity. The Gunn diode supplies the negative resistance that keeps the oscillation going, and the supply voltage and loading only pull the frequency slightly. A Gunn diode oscillator takes advantage of both negative resistance and the bulk effect. It has no PN junction like an ordinary diode. Instead, at high fields, electrons in the bulk of the gallium arsenide transfer to a slower energy band, and that creates the negative resistance.

params.title: Tuning a reflex klystron
rows: Return time of the electron bunches
Fine tuning; what AFC circuits adjust

onScreen: Cavity dimensions: primary frequency, coarse tuning
scenes.narration: A reflex klystron is tuned two ways. Its primary operating frequency is controlled by the dimensions of its resonant cavity, and coarse tuning mechanically changes those dimensions. Fine adjustments are made by varying the repeller voltage. That changes how long the electron bunches take to return to the cavity, which nudges the frequency. Varying the repeller voltage is also what AFC circuits do to keep the klystron on frequency.

params.title: Why CMOS power rises with frequency
labels: Static: CMOS draws almost no current
Every transition charges or discharges the load capacitance
More transitions per second means more power
At high frequencies, CMOS uses almost as much power as TTL

onScreen: High frequency: almost as much as TTL
scenes.narration: Here's a CMOS gate output switching. While it sits still, in a static state, CMOS draws almost no current. But every switching transition charges or discharges the load capacitance, and that takes current. So the faster it switches, the more power it uses: its power rises with switching frequency. That's why, at higher operating frequencies, CMOS circuits consume almost as much power as TTL circuits.

params.title: Analog-to-digital conversion methods
rows: Not a method: dynamic range is a specification

onScreen: Dynamic range: a specification, not a method
scenes.narration: Which of these is not a method of analog-to-digital conversion? Delta-sigma conversion, switched-capacitor conversion and dual-slope integration are all genuine conversion methods. Dynamic-range conversion is not. Dynamic range is a specification: the span of signal levels a converter can handle. It describes a converter, but it isn't a way of converting.

params.title: Blocking oscillator and phantastron
items: Blocking oscillator: T = R × C
Conducts for one brief pulse, then is cut off while C discharges through R
That RC time constant sets the off time, and so the pulse repetition rate
Phantastron: a triggered, one-shot sweep generator
A very linear ramp of precisely settable length, for range-marker and delay timing

onScreen: Brief pulse, then cut off while C discharges
RC sets the off time and PRR
Very linear ramp for range-marker and delay timing
scenes.narration: Two timing circuits. Blocking oscillators operate on the formula T equals R times C. The circuit conducts for one brief pulse, then is held cut off while its timing capacitor discharges through a resistor. That resistor-capacitor time constant sets the off time, and so the pulse repetition rate. The phantastron is a triggered, one-shot sweep generator. When it's triggered by an external source, it develops a very linear ramp voltage, and its length can be set precisely. That makes it useful for range-marker and delay timing.

callouts.label: Memory and I/O interface: the only block on the memory and I/O bus
So it is the memory and I/O that communicate with peripherals
Internal bus: shared, carries one transfer at a time
ALU: arithmetic on data from the general registers and TEMP register
Results return over the internal bus; no address decoding in the ALU

onScreen: Memory and I/O interface on the external bus
Memory and I/O communicate with peripherals
ALU: arithmetic on general register and TEMP data
Result returns over the internal bus
scenes.narration: Figure 8A2 shows a processor's internal blocks. The memory and I-O, or input-output, interface is the only block connected to the external memory and I-O bus. So it's the memory and I-O that communicate with peripherals. Everything else talks over the internal bus, which is shared and carries one transfer at a time. The ALU, the arithmetic logic unit, executes arithmetic manipulations on data from the general registers and the TEMP register, then returns the result over the internal bus. Address decoding and instruction control happen elsewhere, not in the ALU.

callouts.label: Box X: a 51-ohm resistor
It terminates the 50 Ω coax at the receiving end
51 Ω: the nearest standard value to the cable's characteristic impedance
Prevents reflections that would distort the fast digital pulses

onScreen: Nearest standard value to the cable impedance
No reflections to distort the pulses
scenes.narration: In Figure 8A3, digital pulses travel down a 50 ohm coaxial cable. What is the box marked X? It's a 51-ohm resistor, terminating the 50 ohm coax at the receiving end. 51 ohms is the nearest standard value to the cable's characteristic impedance. Terminating the line this way prevents reflections, which would otherwise distort the fast digital pulses.

callouts.label: Filament: heats the cathode and is tied to it
Cathode: pulsed to a high negative voltage
Anode: grounded
So the filament rides at that same high voltage: dangerous

scenes.narration: Which magnetron circuit carries dangerous voltages? The filament. Here's why. The filament heats the cathode and is tied to it. The cathode is pulsed to a high negative voltage, while the anode is grounded. So the whole filament circuit rides at that same high voltage. Don't assume the filament is a low voltage circuit just because it's a heater.

callouts.label: Pins 1 and 4 (clear and preset) held high; both flip-flops reset
Reset: Q low, Q̄ high
Left Q̄ output, pin 6, feeds back to its own data input, pin 2
First clock cycle: the left flip-flop loads a high, so pin 5 goes high
Pin 5 drives the right data input, pin 12; next clock sets pin 9 high
Result: pin 5 high and pin 9 high

scenes.narration: Figure 8A4 shows two D-type flip-flops. Pins 1 and 4, the clear and preset inputs, are held high, and both flip-flops start in the reset state: Q low, and Q bar high. On the left flip-flop, the Q bar output on pin 6 feeds back to its own data input on pin 2. So that input is high, and its first clock cycle loads a high: pin 5 goes high. Pin 5 drives the right flip-flop's data input on pin 12. So the following clock cycle on the right flip-flop sets pin 9 high. The result: pin 5 high, and pin 9 high.

params.title: Photodiode, TTL NAND and address pointers
items: Figure 8A5: the 12 V battery reverse-biases the photodiode, the normal way to run it
Dark: only a tiny dark current. Light makes electron-hole pairs: more light, more current
Figure 8A6, TTL NAND: an input low → Q<sub>1</sub> saturated, Q<sub>2</sub> off, output high
Base current flows out Q<sub>1</sub>'s low emitter; its collector pulls Q<sub>2</sub>'s base low
Figure 8A2: address pointers are in the general registers (data and address registers)

onScreen: 8A5: photodiode reverse-biased by the 12 V battery
8A6: either input low, Q1 saturated, Q2 off, output high
Q1 collector pulls Q2 base low
8A2: address pointers in the general registers
scenes.narration: Three quick figures. In Figure 8A5, the 12 volt battery reverse-biases the photodiode, which is the normal way to run one. In the dark, only a tiny dark current flows. Light creates electron-hole pairs in the junction, so more light means more diode current. Figure 8A6 is a TTL NAND gate. With either input low, base current flows out the low emitter of the multi-emitter transistor Q sub 1. Q sub 1 is saturated, and its collector pulls the base of Q sub 2 low, so Q sub 2 is off and the output goes high. Back in Figure 8A2, address pointers are contained in the general registers, which hold both the data and address registers. The ALU does arithmetic, not address decoding, and the control unit decodes instructions rather than doing arithmetic.

onScreen: R S = (supply − LED voltage) ÷ forward current
scenes.narration: In Figure 8A7, an LED, a light-emitting diode, runs from a 5 volt supply through a series resistor, R sub S. The resistor must drop the supply voltage minus the LED voltage, at the LED's maximum forward current. Here that's 5 volts minus 1.9 volts, divided by 40 milliamps. 5 minus 1.9 is 3.1 volts. 3.1 volts divided by 0.040 amperes is 77.5 ohms, so the answer is about 77 ohms.

callouts.label: Clocked on each low-to-high edge: a D-type flip-flop
Inverting: Qn takes the opposite of Dn, so a high in gives a low out
A high on the active-low output enable forces Z, the high-impedance state
So it is 3-state
D-type flip-flop, 3-state, inverting

onScreen: Output enable high: Z, high impedance
scenes.narration: Last, Figure 8A8, a truth table for a part on a RADAR circuit board. Look at the rows with a low-to-high clock edge. On each one, the output Q n takes the opposite of the data input D n: a high in gives a low out. So it's a D-type flip-flop, and it's inverting. Now the bottom row: a high on the active-low output enable forces the output to Z, the high-impedance state. That makes it 3-state. Put together: a D-type flip-flop, 3-state, inverting.
